# Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration

## Introduction​

WooCommerce registers product and order abilities in WordPress. With the MCP Adapter plugin, AI clients can discover and run these store operations through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), subject to WordPress and WooCommerce permissions.

info

Developer Preview Notice The MCP implementation in WooCommerce is currently in developer preview. Implementation details, APIs, and integration patterns may change in future releases as the feature matures.

## Enabling MCP Integration​

WooCommerce always registers its abilities through the WordPress Abilities API; there is no WooCommerce setting to turn on. To make them available to MCP clients, install and activate the MCP Adapter plugin:
    
    `
    
    wp plugin install mcp-adapter --activate
    
    `

WooCommerce does not bundle the MCP adapter.

## Authentication and Security​

### WordPress Application Password Requirements​

Remote HTTP connections authenticate using a WordPress username and an Application Password. Do not use your account password or a WooCommerce REST API key.

To create an Application Password:

  1. In the WordPress dashboard, navigate to Users → Profile.
  2. Under Application Passwords, enter a name for the MCP client.
  3. Click Add New Application Password.
  4. Copy the generated password and store it securely. WordPress only displays it once.

Use the WordPress username and generated password as `WP_API_USERNAME` and `WP_API_PASSWORD` in the remote proxy conf

pages.text: Authentication | WooCommerce developer docs Skip to main content On this page Copy markdown Copies the current page content as markdown format to your clipboard WooCommerce includes two ways to authenticate with the WP REST API. It is also possible to authenticate using any WP REST API authentication plugin or method. REST API keys ​ Pre-generated keys can be used to authenticate use of the REST API endpoints. New keys can be generated either through the WordPress admin interface or they can be auto-generated through an endpoint. Generating API keys in the WordPress admin interface ​ To create or manage keys for a specific WordPress user, go to WooCommerce > Settings > Advanced > REST API. Note: Keys/Apps was found at WooCommerce > Settings > API > Key/Apps prior to WooCommerce 3.4. Click the "Add Key" button. In the next screen, add a description and select the WordPress user you would like to generate the key for. Use of the REST API with the generated keys will conform to that user's WordPress roles and capabilities. Choose the level of access for this REST API key, which can be Read access, Write access or Read/Write access. Then click the "Generate API Key" button and WooCommerce will generate REST API keys for the selected user. Now that keys have been generated, you should see two new keys, a QRCode, and a Revoke API Key button. These two keys are your Consumer Key and Consumer Secret. If the WordPress user associated with an API key is deleted, the API key will cease to function. API keys are not transferred to other users. Auto generating API keys using our Application Authentication Endpoint ​ This endpoint can be used by any APP to allow users to generate API keys for your APP. This makes integration with WooCommerce API easier because the user only needs to grant access to your APP via a URL. After being redirected back to your APP, the API keys will be sent back in a separate POST request. The following image illustrates how this works: warning This endpoint works exclusively for users to generate API keys and facilitate integration between the WooCommerce REST API and an application. In no way is this endpoint intended to be used as login method for customers. URL parameters ​ Parameter Type Description app_name string Your APP name MANDATORY scope string Level of access. Available: read , write and read_write MANDATORY user_id string User ID in your APP. For your internal reference, used when the user is redirected back to your APP. NOT THE USER ID IN WOOCOMMERCE MANDATORY return_url string URL the user will be redirected to after authentication MANDATORY callback_url string URL that will receive the generated API key. Note: this URL should be over HTTPS MANDATORY Creating an authentication endpoint URL ​ You must use the /wc-auth/v1/authorize endpoint and pass the above parameters as a query string. Example of how to build an authentication URL: cURL JavaScript PHP Python Ruby # Bash example STORE_URL='http://example.com' ENDPOINT='/wc-auth/v1/authorize' PARAMS="app_name=My App Name&scope=read_write&user_id=123&return_url=http://app.com/return-page&callback_url=https://app.com/callback-endpoint" QUERY_STRING="$(perl -MURI::Escape -e 'print uri_escape($ARGV[0]);' "$PARAMS")" QUERY_STRING=$(echo $QUERY_STRING | sed -e "s/%20/\+/g" -e "s/%3D/\=/g" -e "s/%26/\&/g") echo "$STORE_URL$ENDPOINT?$QUERY_STRING" const querystring = require ( 'querystring' ) ; const store_url = 'http://example.com' ; const endpoint = '/wc-auth/v1/authorize' ; const params = { app_name : 'My App Name' , scope : 'read_write' , user_id : 123 , return_url : 'http://app.com/return-page' , callback_url : 'https://app.com/callback-endpoint' } ; const query_string = querystring . stringify ( params ) . replace ( / %20 / g , '+' ) ; console . log ( store_url + endpoint + '?' + query_string ) ; <?php $store_url = 'http://example.com' ; $endpoint = '/wc-auth/v1/authorize' ; $params = [ 'app_name' => 'My App Name' , 'scope' => 'write' , 'user_id' => 123 , 'return_url' => 'http://app.com' , 'callback_url' => 'https://app.com' ] ; $query_string = http_build_query ( $params ) ; echo $store_url . $endpoint . '?' . $query_string ; ?> from urllib . parse import urlencode store_url = 'http://example.com' endpoint = '/wc-auth/v1/authorize' params = { "app_name" : "My App Name" , "scope" : "read_write" , "user_id" : 123 , "return_url" : "http://app.com/return-page" , "callback_url" : "https://app.com/callback-endpoint" } query_string = urlencode ( params ) print ( "%s%s?%s" % ( store_url , endpoint , query_string ) ) require "uri" store_url = 'http://example.com' endpoint = '/wc-auth/v1/authorize' params = { app_name: "My App Name", scope: "read_write", user_id: 123, return_url: "http://app.com/return-page", callback_url: "https://app.com/callback-endpoint" } query_string = URI.encode_www_form(params) puts "#{store_url}#{endpoint}?#{query_string}" Example of JSON posted with the API Keys { "key_id": 1, "user_id": 123, "consumer_key": "ck_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", "consumer_secret": "cs_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx", "key_permissions": "read_write" } Example of the screen that the user will see: Notes ​ While redirecting the user using return_url , you are also sent success and user_id parameters as query strings. success sends 0 if the user denied, or 1 if authenticated successfully. Use user_id to identify the user when redirected back to the ( return_url ) and also remember to save the API Keys when your callback_url is posted to after auth. The auth endpoint will send the API Keys in JSON format to the callback_url , so it's important to remember that some languages such as PHP will not display it inside the $_POST global variable, in PHP you can access it using $HTTP_RAW_POST_DATA (for old PHP versions) or file_get_contents('php://input'); . The URL generated must have all query string values encoded. Authentication over HTTPS ​ You may use HTTP Basic Auth by providing the REST API Consumer Key as the username and the REST API Consumer Secret as the password. HTTP Basic Auth example cURL JavaScript PHP Python Ruby curl https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/orders \ -u consumer_key:consumer_secret const WooCommerceRestApi = require ( "@woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api" ) . default ; // import WooCommerceRestApi from "@woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api"; // Supports ESM const WooCommerce = new WooCommerceRestApi ( { url : 'https://example.com' , consumerKey : 'consumer_key' , consumerSecret : 'consumer_secret' , version : 'wc/v3' } ) ; <?php require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php' ; use Automattic \ WooCommerce \ Client ; $woocommerce = new Client ( 'https://example.com' , 'consumer_key' , 'consumer_secret' , [ 'wp_api' => true , 'version' => 'wc/v3' ] ) ; ?> from woocommerce import API wcapi = API ( url = "https://example.com" , consumer_key = "consumer_key" , consumer_secret = "consumer_secret" , wp_api = True , version = "wc/v3" ) require "woocommerce_api" woocommerce = WooCommerce::API.new( "https://example.com", "consumer_key", "consumer_secret", { wp_json: true, version: "wc/v3" } ) Occasionally some servers may not parse the Authorization header correctly (if you see a "Consumer key is missing" error when authenticating over SSL, you have a server issue). In this case, you may provide the consumer key/secret as query string parameters instead. Example for servers that not properly parse the Authorization header: cURL JavaScript PHP Python Ruby curl https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/orders?consumer_key=123&consumer_secret=abc const WooCommerceRestApi = require ( "@woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api" ) . default ; // import WooCommerceRestApi from "@woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api"; // Supports ESM const WooCommerce = new WooCommerceRestApi ( { url : 'https://example.com' , consumerKey : 'consumer_key' , consumerSecret : 'consumer_secret' , version : 'wc/v3' , queryStringAuth : true // Force Basic Authentication as query string true and using under HTTPS } ) ; <?php require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php' ; use Automattic \ WooCommerce \ Client ; $woocommerce = new Client ( 'https://example.com' , 'consumer_key' , 'consumer_secret' , [ 'wp_api' => true , 'version' => 'wc/v3' , 'query_string_auth' => true // Force Basic Authentication as query string true and using under HTTPS ] ) ; ?> from woocommerce import API wcapi = API ( url = "https://example.com" , consumer_key = "consumer_key" , consumer_secret = "consumer_secret" , wp_api = True , version = "wc/v3" , query_string_auth = True # Force Basic Authentication as query string true and using under HTTPS ) require "woocommerce_api" woocommerce = WooCommerce::API.new( "https://example.com", "consumer_key", "consumer_secret", { wp_json: true, version: "wc/v3", query_string_auth: true  # Force Basic Authentication as query string true and using under HTTPS } ) Authentication over HTTP ​ You must use OAuth 1.0a "one-legged" authentication to ensure REST API credentials cannot be intercepted by an attacker. Typically you will use any standard OAuth 1.0a library in the language of your choice to handle the authentication, or generate the necessary parameters by following the following instructions. Creating a signature ​ Collect the request method and URL ​ First you need to determine the HTTP method you will be using for the request, and the URL of the request. The HTTP method will be GET in our case. The Request URL will be the endpoint you are posting to, e.g. http://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/orders . Collect parameters ​ Collect and normalize your parameters. This includes all oauth_* parameters except for the oauth_signature itself. These values need to be encoded into a single string which will be used later on. The process to build the string is very specific: Percent encode every key and value that will be signed. Sort the list of parameters alphabetically by encoded key. For each key/value pair: Append the encoded key to the output string. Append the = character to the output string. Append the encoded value to the output string. If there are more key/value pairs remaining, append a & character to the output string. When percent encoding in PHP for example, you would use rawurlencode() . When sorting parameters in PHP for example, you would use uksort( $params, 'strcmp' ) . Parameters example: oauth_consumer_key=abc123&oauth_signature_method=HMAC-SHA1 Create the signature base string ​ The above values collected so far must be joined to make a single string, from which the signature will be generated. This is called the signature base string in the OAuth specification. To encode the HTTP method, request URL, and parameter string into a single string: Set the output string equal to the uppercase HTTP Method . Append the & character to the output string. Percent encode the URL and append it to the output string. Append the & character to the output string. Percent encode the parameter string and append it to the output string. Example signature base string: GET&http%3A%2F%2Fwww.example.com%2Fwp-json%2Fwc%2Fv3%2Forders&oauth_consumer_key%3Dabc123%26oauth_signature_method%3DHMAC-SHA1 Generate the signature ​ Generate the signature using the signature base string and your consumer secret key with a & character with the HMAC-SHA1 hashing algorithm. In PHP you can use the hash_hmac function. HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-SHA256 are the only accepted hash algorithms. If you are having trouble generating a correct signature, you'll want to review the string you are signing for encoding errors. The authentication source can also be helpful in understanding how to properly generate the signature. OAuth tips ​ The OAuth parameters may be added as query string parameters or included in the Authorization header. Note there is no reliable cross-platform way to get the raw request headers in WordPress, so query string should be more reliable in some cases. The required parameters are: oauth_consumer_key , oauth_timestamp , oauth_nonce , oauth_signature , and oauth_signature_method . oauth_version is not required and should be omitted. The OAuth nonce can be any randomly generated 32 character (recommended) string that is unique to the consumer key. The OAuth timestamp should be the unix timestamp at the time of the request. The REST API will deny any requests that include a timestamp outside of a 15 minute window to prevent replay attacks. You must use the store URL provided by the index when forming the base string used for the signature, as this is what the server will use. (e.g. if the store URL includes a www sub-domain, you should use it for requests) Note that the request body is not signed as per the OAuth spec. If including parameters in your request, it saves a lot of trouble if you can order your items alphabetically. Authorization header is supported starting WooCommerce 3.0. pages.text: WooCommerce REST API | WooCommerce developer docs Skip to main content On this page Copy markdown Copies the current page content as markdown format to your clipboard WooCommerce (WC) 2.6+ is fully integrated with the WordPress REST API. This allows WC data to be created, read, updated, and deleted using requests in JSON format and using WordPress REST API Authentication methods and standard HTTP verbs which are understood by most HTTP clients. The current WP REST API integration version is v3 which takes a first-order position in endpoints. When WooPayments is active, it adds payment-specific endpoints under /wp-json/wc/v3/payments/ . See the WooPayments REST API reference for transactions, authorizations, and payouts. Some monetary fields in these endpoints use integer minor units, unlike WooCommerce core's decimal-string values. Requirements ​ To use the REST API you must be using: WooCommerce 3.5+ WordPress 4.4+ Pretty permalinks in Settings > Permalinks (default permalinks will not work) You may access the API over either HTTP or HTTPS, but HTTPS is recommended where possible . note You are not required to install the WP REST API (WP API) plugin. If you use ModSecurity and see 501 Method Not Implemented errors, see this issue for details. Libraries and tools ​ Official libraries ​ JavaScript Library PHP Library Python Library Ruby Library JavaScript PHP Python Ruby // Install: // npm install --save @woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api // Setup: const WooCommerceRestApi = require ( "@woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api" ) . default ; // import WooCommerceRestApi from "@woocommerce/woocommerce-rest-api"; // Supports ESM const WooCommerce = new WooCommerceRestApi ( { url : 'http://example.com' , // Your store URL consumerKey : 'consumer_key' , // Your consumer key consumerSecret : 'consumer_secret' , // Your consumer secret version : 'wc/v3' // WooCommerce WP REST API version } ) ; <?php // Install: // composer require automattic/woocommerce // Setup: require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php' ; use Automattic \ WooCommerce \ Client ; $woocommerce = new Client ( 'http://example.com' , // Your store URL 'consumer_key' , // Your consumer key 'consumer_secret' , // Your consumer secret [ 'wp_api' => true , // Enable the WP REST API integration 'version' => 'wc/v3' // WooCommerce WP REST API version ] ) ; ?> # Install: # pip install woocommerce # Setup: from woocommerce import API wcapi = API ( url = "http://example.com" , # Your store URL consumer_key = "consumer_key" , # Your consumer key consumer_secret = "consumer_secret" , # Your consumer secret wp_api = True , # Enable the WP REST API integration version = "wc/v3" # WooCommerce WP REST API version ) # Install: # gem install woocommerce_api # Setup: require "woocommerce_api" woocommerce = WooCommerce::API.new( "https://example.com", # Your store URL "consumer_key", # Your consumer key "consumer_secret", # Your consumer secret { wp_api: true, # Enable the WP REST API integration version: "wc/v3" # WooCommerce WP REST API version } ) Third party libraries ​ Java Library .NET Library Android Library note We don't offer support for third party libraries. If you have questions about how to use any of these libraries, contact the respective authors. Tools ​ Insomnia - Cross-platform GraphQL and REST client, available for Mac, Windows, and Linux. Postman - Cross-platform REST client, available for Mac, Windows, and Linux. RequestBin - Allows you test webhooks. Hookbin - Another tool to test webhooks. Generate keys ​ To start using REST API, you first need to generate API keys. Go to WooCommerce > Settings > Advanced Go to the REST API tab and click Add key Give the key a description for your own reference, choose a user with access to orders etc, and give the key read/write permissions Click Generate API key Your keys will be shown - do not close this tab yet, the secret will be hidden if you try to view the key again Make a basic request ​ The request URL we'll test is wp-json/wc/v3/orders . On localhost the full URL may look something like this: https://localhost:8888/wp-json/wc/v3/orders . Modify this to use your own site URL. In Postman, you need to set the fields for request type, request URL, and the settings on the authorization tab. For Authorization, choose basic auth and enter your consumer key and consumer secret keys from WooCommerce into the username and password fields. Once done, hit send and you'll see the JSON response from the API if all worked well: Insomnia is almost identical to Postman; fill in the same fields and again use basic auth: Request/Response format ​ The default response format is JSON. Requests with a message-body use plain JSON to set or update resource attributes. Successful requests will return a 200 OK HTTP status. Some general information about responses: Dates are returned in ISO8601 format: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS Resource IDs are returned as integers Any decimal monetary amount, such as prices or totals, will be returned as strings with two decimal places Other amounts, such as item counts, are returned as integers Blank fields are generally included as null or empty string instead of being omitted JSONP support ​ The WP REST API supports JSONP by default. JSONP responses use the application/javascript content-type. You can specify the callback using the ?_jsonp parameter for GET requests to have the response wrapped in a JSON function: GET /wp-json/wc/v3?_jsonp=callback Parameters ​ Almost all endpoints accept optional parameters which can be passed as a HTTP query string parameter, e.g. GET /orders?status=completed . All parameters are documented along each endpoint. Pagination ​ Requests that return multiple items will be paginated to 10 items by default. This default can be changed by the site administrator by changing the posts_per_page option. Alternatively the items per page can be specified with the ?per_page parameter: GET /orders?per_page=15 You can specify further pages with the ?page parameter: GET /orders?page=2 You may also specify the offset from the first resource using the ?offset parameter: GET /orders?offset=5 Page number is 1-based and omitting the ?page parameter will return the first page. The total number of resources and pages are always included in the X-WP-Total and X-WP-TotalPages HTTP headers. Link header ​ Pagination info is included in the Link Header . It's recommended that you follow these values instead of building your own URLs where possible. Link: <https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products?page=2>; rel="next", <https://www.example.com/wp-json/wc/v3/products?page=3>; rel="last" Value Description next Shows the URL of the immediate next page of results. last Shows the URL of the last page of results. first Shows the URL of the first page of results. prev Shows the URL of the immediate previous page of results. Errors ​ Occasionally you might encounter errors when accessing the REST API. There are four possible types: Error Code Error Type 400 Bad Request Invalid request, e.g. using an unsupported HTTP method 401 Unauthorized Authentication or permission error, e.g. incorrect API keys 404 Not Found Requests to resources that don't exist or are missing 500 Internal Server Error Server error Errors return both an appropriate HTTP status code and response object which contains a code , message and data attribute: { "code" : "woocommerce_rest_term_invalid" , "message" : "Resource doesn't exist." , "data" : { "status" : 404 } } Common connection issues ​ Connection issues with localhost and self-signed SSL certificates ​ If you're having problems connecting to the REST API on your localhost and seeing SSL errors, you need to disable SSL verification. In Postman you can find this in the settings: Insomnia also has this setting in the preferences area: 401 Unauthorized ​ Your API keys or signature is wrong. Ensure that: The user you generated API keys for actually has access to those resources The username when authenticating is your consumer key The password when authenticating is your consumer secret Make a new set of keys to be sure If your server utilizes FastCGI, check that your authorization headers are properly read . Consumer key is missing ​ Occasionally servers may not parse the Authorization header correctly (if you see a "Consumer key is missing" error when authenticating over SSL, you have a server issue). In this case, you may provide the consumer key/secret as query string parameters instead: https://local.wordpress.dev/wp-json/wc/v2/orders?consumer_key=XXXX&consumer_secret=XXXX Server does not support POST/DELETE/PUT ​ Ideally, your server should be configured to accept these types of API request, but if not you can use the _method property . API version history ​ API Version WC Version WP Version v3 3.5.x or later 4.4 or later v2 3.0.x or later 4.4 or later v1 2.6.x or later 4.4 or later Learn more ​ Learn more about the REST API checking the official WordPress REST API documentation . Requirements Libraries and tools Official libraries Third party libraries Tools Generate keys Make a basic request Request/Response format JSONP support Parameters Pagination Link header Errors Common connection issues Connection issues with localhost and self-signed SSL certificates 401 Unauthorized Consumer key is missing Server does not support POST/DELETE/PUT API version history Learn more Use of your personal data We and our partners process your personal data (such as browsing data, IP Addresses, cookie information, and other unique identifiers) based on your consent and/or our legitimate interest to optimize our website, marketing activities, and your user experience. pages.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration | WooCommerce developer docs (https://developer.woocommerce.com/docs/features/mcp/)
pages.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration | WooCommerce developer docs Skip to main content On this page Copy markdown Copies the current page content as markdown format to your clipboard Introduction ​ WooCommerce registers product and order abilities in WordPress. With the MCP Adapter plugin, AI clients can discover and run these store operations through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), subject to WordPress and WooCommerce permissions. info Developer Preview Notice The MCP implementation in WooCommerce is currently in developer preview. Implementation details, APIs, and integration patterns may change in future releases as the feature matures. Enabling MCP Integration ​ WooCommerce always registers its abilities through the WordPress Abilities API; there is no WooCommerce setting to turn on. To make them available to MCP clients, install and activate the MCP Adapter plugin : wp plugin install mcp-adapter --activate WooCommerce does not bundle the MCP adapter. Authentication and Security ​ WordPress Application Password Requirements ​ Remote HTTP connections authenticate using a WordPress username and an Application Password . Do not use your account password or a WooCommerce REST API key. To create an Application Password: In the WordPress dashboard, navigate to Users → Profile . Under Application Passwords , enter a name for the MCP client. Click Add New Application Password . Copy the generated password and store it securely. WordPress only displays it once. Use the WordPress username and generated password as WP_API_USERNAME and WP_API_PASSWORD in the remote proxy configuration. Application Passwords can be revoked independently from the user's profile. HTTPS Enforcement ​ Use HTTPS for remote HTTP connections so credentials are encrypted in transit. Local STDIO connections authenticate through WP-CLI using the configured --user and do not require an Application Password. Permission Validation ​ The MCP Adapter authenticates requests as the WordPress user associated with the Application Password. The default server requires an authenticated user with the read capability, and each WooCommerce ability also enforces its own permission callback. Use a dedicated WordPress user with only the capabilities the MCP client needs. Server Endpoint ​ WooCommerce abilities are available through the WordPress MCP Adapter's default server: https://yourstore.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server The WooCommerce-specific /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp endpoint was removed in WooCommerce 11.3. See Removed in WooCommerce 11.3 . Connecting to the MCP Server ​ Choose a connection method based on where the WordPress site is running. For a detailed overview and application-specific instructions, see Connecting AI applications and the wordpress/mcp-adaptor repository . Local Sites Using STDIO ​ For a local WordPress installation, MCP clients can connect directly through the MCP Adapter's WP-CLI command. The client needs access to the WordPress files and a working WP-CLI installation. JSON Configuration ​ Add the following server to your MCP client configuration. Replace the WordPress path and user with values from your local environment: { "mcpServers" : { "woocommerce_store" : { "command" : "wp" , "args" : [ "--path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site" , "mcp-adapter" , "serve" , "--server=mcp-adapter-default-server" , "--user=admin" ] } } } Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and Cursor use the mcpServers property shown above. For VS Code, use servers instead. Command-Line Configuration ​ Claude Code users can add the same server from the command line: claude mcp add woocommerce_store -- \ wp --path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site \ mcp-adapter serve \ --server=mcp-adapter-default-server \ --user=admin You can verify the server directly with WP-CLI: echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}' | \ wp --path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site \ mcp-adapter serve \ --server=mcp-adapter-default-server \ --user=admin Remote Sites Using HTTP ​ For a remote WordPress installation, use the @automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote proxy. The proxy translates the MCP client's local STDIO messages into HTTP requests to the WordPress MCP Adapter. Before connecting: Create or select a dedicated WordPress user with the minimum required capabilities. Open the user's Profile screen and create a WordPress Application Password. Confirm the site uses HTTPS and non-Plain permalinks. JSON Configuration ​ Add the following server to your MCP client configuration. Replace the example URL, username, and Application Password: { "mcpServers" : { "woocommerce_store" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "-y" , "@automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote@latest" ] , "env" : { "WP_API_URL" : "https://yourstore.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server" , "WP_API_USERNAME" : "your-username" , "WP_API_PASSWORD" : "your-application-password" } } } } Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and Cursor use the mcpServers property shown above. For VS Code, use servers instead. Do not commit a configuration containing an Application Password to version control. Command-Line Configuration ​ Claude Code users can add the remote server from the command line: claude mcp add \ --env WP_API_URL=https://yourstore.com/wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server \ --env WP_API_USERNAME=your-username \ --env WP_API_PASSWORD='your-application-password' \ woocommerce_store \ -- npx -y @automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote@latest Troubleshooting : For common setup issues with npx versions or SSL in local environments, see the mcp-wordpress-remote troubleshooting guide . Discover WooCommerce Abilities ​ The default MCP server exposes three tools: mcp-adapter-discover-abilities , mcp-adapter-get-ability-info , and mcp-adapter-execute-ability . A tools/list response shows these adapter tools, not a separate tool for each WooCommerce ability. Use the discovery tool to list available abilities, then get an ability's schema before executing it. For a local site, you can check discovery with WP-CLI: echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"mcp-adapter-discover-abilities","arguments":{}}}' | \ wp --path=/path/to/your/wordpress/site \ mcp-adapter serve \ --server=mcp-adapter-default-server \ --user=admin On a WooCommerce 11.3 site, the response should include abilities such as woocommerce/products-query and woocommerce/order-notes-query . Each ability checks permissions when it runs. See the MCP Adapter default server guide for the discovery and execution flow. Background ​ The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI applications to securely connect to external data sources and tools. Using MCP with WooCommerce relies on two core technologies: WordPress Abilities API - A standardized system for registering capabilities in WordPress, included in WordPress core WordPress MCP Adapter - The core MCP protocol implementation, installed as the MCP Adapter plugin This architecture allows WooCommerce to expose operations as MCP tools through the flexible WordPress Abilities system while maintaining existing security and permission models. What's Available ​ WooCommerce registers purpose-built abilities for core store operations. These abilities are available through the WordPress Abilities API and can be surfaced through the shared WordPress MCP adapter. Purpose-Built WooCommerce Abilities ​ Product Management ​ Query products with filtering and pagination Create new products Update existing products Delete products Order Management ​ Query orders with filtering and pagination Query notes for an order ( woocommerce/order-notes-query ) Update order status Add order notes All operations respect WooCommerce's existing permission system. MCP clients authenticate through the MCP Adapter as a WordPress user. Removed in WooCommerce 11.3 ​ WooCommerce 11.3 removed the deprecated WooCommerce MCP endpoint and everything that only existed to support it: The /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp endpoint and its WooCommerce REST API key authentication ( X-MCP-API-Key ). Requests to the endpoint now return HTTP 410 with a JSON-RPC error that explains how to connect through the MCP Adapter. The REST-derived product and order abilities ( woocommerce/products-list , woocommerce/orders-get , and similar), along with the woocommerce_mcp_include_ability , woocommerce_mcp_allow_insecure_transport , and woocommerce_check_rest_ability_permissions_for_method filters and the expose_in_deprecated_woocommerce_mcp ability metadata. Custom abilities registered by extensions or custom code that appeared in the removed endpoint don't carry over automatically. Before WooCommerce 10.9, the endpoint included abilities in the woocommerce/ namespace; from 10.9, it included abilities with expose_in_deprecated_woocommerce_mcp set to true ; and the woocommerce_mcp_include_ability filter could add or remove abilities in either version. The MCP Adapter's default server ignores all of these. It only exposes an ability when its meta.mcp.public is true (if meta.mcp.public is not set, the adapter falls back to the top-level meta.public ). To keep a custom ability available to MCP clients, set that metadata as shown in Adding Custom Abilities . To keep using WooCommerce with MCP, install the MCP Adapter plugin and connect your MCP client to its default server, as described in Connecting to the MCP Server . Stores that had the WooCommerce MCP feature enabled see an admin notice about the change. warning Data Privacy Notice Order and customer operations may expose personally identifiable information (PII) including names, email addresses, physical addresses, and payment details. You are responsible for ensuring compliance with applicable data protection regulations. Connect MCP clients as a dedicated WordPress user with only the capabilities they need, revoke Application Passwords you no longer use, and follow your organization's data retention and handling policies. Architecture ​ Data Flow Overview ​ The MCP integration uses a multi-layered architecture to bridge between MCP clients and WordPress: AI Client (Claude, etc.) ↓ (MCP protocol over stdio/JSON-RPC) Local MCP Proxy (mcp-wordpress-remote) ↓ (HTTP/HTTPS requests with authentication) Remote WordPress MCP Server (mcp-adapter) ↓ (WordPress Abilities API) WooCommerce Abilities ↓ (REST API calls or direct operations) WooCommerce Core Architecture Components ​ Local MCP Proxy ( mcp-wordpress-remote ) Runs locally on the developer's machine as a Node.js process Converts MCP protocol messages to HTTP requests Handles authentication header injection Bridges the protocol gap between MCP clients and WordPress REST endpoints Remote WordPress MCP Server ( mcp-adapter ) Is provided by the MCP Adapter plugin , which must be installed and active Powers MCP tool discovery and execution for WordPress abilities WordPress Abilities System ​ Provides a standardized way to register and execute capabilities Acts as an abstraction layer between MCP tools and actual operations Enables flexible implementation approaches (direct operations, REST bridging, and so on) Core Components ​ Purpose-Built Domain Abilities ( Domain ) Provide WooCommerce product and order abilities backed by domain APIs Use shared WordPress MCP adapter metadata ( mcp.public and mcp.type ) for MCP exposure Keep the ability contract focused on agent-friendly store operations Implementation Approach ​ WooCommerce implements its abilities as purpose-built domain abilities. These abilities use schemas and response shapes designed for agent workflows instead of automatically projecting every REST-shaped operation into MCP. Extending MCP Capabilities ​ Third-party plugins can register additional abilities using the WordPress Abilities API. Abilities can be implemented in various ways, including direct operations, custom logic, REST endpoint bridging, or external integrations. Adding Custom Abilities ​ Register an ability category first, then register the ability during the WordPress Abilities API init hook: add_action ( 'wp_abilities_api_categories_init' , function ( ) { if ( ! function_exists ( 'wp_register_ability_category' ) ) { return ; } if ( function_exists ( 'wp_has_ability_category' ) && wp_has_ability_category ( 'your-plugin' ) ) { return ; } wp_register_ability_category ( 'your-plugin' , array ( 'label' => __ ( 'Your Plugin' , 'your-plugin' ) , 'description' => __ ( 'Abilities provided by Your Plugin.' , 'your-plugin' ) , ) ) ; } ) ; add_action ( 'wp_abilities_api_init' , function ( ) { if ( ! function_exists ( 'wp_register_ability' ) ) { return ; } wp_register_ability ( 'your-plugin/custom-operation' , array ( 'label' => __ ( 'Custom Store Operation' , 'your-plugin' ) , 'description' => __ ( 'Performs a custom store operation.' , 'your-plugin' ) , 'category' => 'your-plugin' , 'execute_callback' => 'your_custom_ability_handler' , 'permission_callback' => function ( ) { return current_user_can ( 'manage_woocommerce' ) ; } , 'input_schema' => array ( 'type' => 'object' , 'properties' => array ( 'store_id' => array ( 'type' => 'integer' , 'description' => 'Store identifier' , ) , ) , 'required' => array ( 'store_id' ) , ) , 'output_schema' => array ( 'type' => 'object' , 'properties' => array ( 'success' => array ( 'type' => 'boolean' , 'description' => 'Operation result' , ) , ) , ) , 'meta' => array ( 'show_in_rest' => true , 'mcp' => array ( 'public' => true , 'type' => 'tool' , ) , ) , ) ) ; } ) ; The mcp.public and mcp.type metadata tells the shared WordPress MCP adapter that the ability can be exposed as an MCP tool. The show_in_rest metadata exposes the ability through the Abilities API REST routes. Development Example ​ For a complete working example, see the WooCommerce MCP Ability Demo Plugin . This demonstration plugin shows how third-party developers can: Register custom abilities using the WordPress Abilities API Define comprehensive input and output schemas Implement proper permission handling Integrate with MCP through the shared WordPress MCP adapter The demo plugin creates a woocommerce-demo/store-info ability that retrieves store information and statistics, demonstrating the integration patterns for extending WooCommerce MCP capabilities while using a direct implementation approach rather than REST endpoint bridging. Troubleshooting ​ Common Issues ​ MCP Server Not Available ​ Verify the MCP Adapter plugin is installed and active Confirm the client connects to /wp-json/mcp/mcp-adapter-default-server , not the removed /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp endpoint Authentication Failures ​ Confirm WP_API_USERNAME matches the WordPress user that created the Application Password Confirm WP_API_PASSWORD contains an active Application Password, not the user's account password or a WooCommerce REST API key Verify the WordPress user has the capabilities required by the ability Ensure HTTPS is used for remote HTTP connections Ability Not Found ​ Confirm the ability category is registered during wp_abilities_api_categories_init Confirm abilities are registered during wp_abilities_api_init Verify ability callbacks are accessible Check WooCommerce → Status → Logs for entries with source woocommerce-abilities . Important Considerations ​ Developer Preview : This feature is in preview status and may change Implementation Approach : WooCommerce uses purpose-built domain abilities Breaking Changes : Future updates may introduce breaking changes Production Testing : Thoroughly test before deploying to production API Stability : The WordPress Abilities API and MCP adapter are evolving Related Resources ​ WordPress Abilities API Repository WordPress MCP Adapter Repository WooCommerce MCP Demo Plugin Model Context Protocol Specification WooCommerce REST API Documentation Introduction Enabling MCP Integration Authentication and Security WordPress Application Password Requirements HTTPS Enforcement Permission Validation Server Endpoint Connecting to the MCP Server Local Sites Using STDIO Remote Sites Using HTTP Discover WooCommerce Abilities Background What's Available Purpose-Built WooCommerce Abilities Removed in WooCommerce 11.3 Architecture Data Flow Overview Architecture Components Core Components Implementation Approach Extending MCP Capabilities Adding Custom Abilities Development Example Troubleshooting Common Issues MCP Server Not Available Authentication Failures Ability Not Found Important Considerations Related Resources Use of your personal data We and our partners process your personal data (such as browsing data, IP Addresses, cookie information, and other unique identifiers) based on your consent and/or our legitimate interest to optimize our website, marketing activities, and your user experience. Retired Products Expand Woo Marketplace Code Snippets Expand MCP for WooCommerce MCP for WooCommerce by w7s connects Claude , ChatGPT , and other AI assistants to your WooCommerce store so they can work with your orders, products, customers, and more in plain language. It runs its own Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on the free MCP Adapter plugin, gives you a settings screen to manage the connection and your API keys, and lets you choose exactly which groups of tools the AI client is allowed to use. This guide covers what you need, how to set it up, what every setting does, and how developers can extend it. MCP for WooCommerce gives your store its own MCP server. MCP is the standard that lets an AI assistant call tools on your site. The plugin’s server lives at /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/mcp and runs on the MCP Adapter, a free plugin from WordPress.org that handles the MCP protocol for WordPress. It does three main things: It provides a settings area under WooCommerce > Settings > MCP for connecting an assistant, creating API keys, and reviewing activity; It registers a large set of MCP abilities so an assistant can list and manage orders, products, customers, coupons, refunds, tax, shipping, webhooks, reports, and more; and It lets you switch whole groups of tools (called tool packs) on or off, so an assistant only ever sees the capabilities you have chosen to expose. On top of the server, the plugin adds the connection and key management screens, a large library of abilities, tool pack gating that is enforced when a tool runs, optional activity logging and change history, and API key permission enforcement on every call. It does not depend on WooCommerce’s own MCP feature, which WooCommerce removes in version 11.3. Once the MCP Adapter is active and MCP for WooCommerce’s server answers, WooCommerce’s notice is retired. On WooCommerce 11.3 and later, the Connection tab keeps a short note in its place: “WooCommerce 11.3 moved AI connections to the MCP Adapter plugin. An Application Password carries every permission of the user it belongs to, and has no read-only option. Each person can have their own. Every key can be revoked on its own, and the action log records who used which one. Your existing connections already use them. The nine core product and order tools keep their names. You can turn them on in the WooCommerce built-in abilities pack. The sections below follow the tabs in the order you will use them. On a public site that step is skipped, and the steps that follow move up by one. The Connection tab is where you link an assistant to your store. It opens with the MCP Adapter status and the connector switch, followed by numbered steps: MCP Adapter status. Shown only when the adapter needs attention: what is wrong and the button to fix it. See The MCP Adapter . WooCommerce 11.3 note. On WooCommerce 11.3 and later, while an adapter is loaded, a line under the status reads: “WooCommerce 11.3 moved AI connections to the MCP Adapter plugin. MCP for WooCommerce connects through it, so your existing AI connections keep working.”, with a Why this changed link. Enable MCP for WooCommerce connector. The master switch for the whole integration. When it is off, no tools and no keys are exposed to any assistant, and the Tool Packs, Add tools, Store Control, and Activity tabs are hidden. Changes to this switch are saved immediately. With the connector on, the steps are: Select your environment (local sites only) — choose between a public website (accessible on the internet) and a local website (on your computer). On a public site this step is skipped. Select your AI assistant — choose Claude (Recommended) , ChatGPT / Codex , Cursor , VS Code / GitHub Copilot , or Other AI service . Only the methods that work for your assistant and environment are shown. The exact steps are covered in Connecting an assistant below. Under the connect step, the plugin watches for the new key’s first authenticated use. If nothing arrives for a while, it suggests checking that the app finished its setup, with a Check again button. The Advanced tab holds the settings you rarely need while connecting for the first time: logging, how long Claude connector sessions are kept, site readiness, and the API key list. It is always shown, even with the connector off, so you can check your site before you switch it on. Logging. These settings are shown while the connector is on: Log AI assistant actions records MCP tool calls. It is on by default. Keep logs for (days) sets how long entries are kept, from 1 to 365. The default is 7 days, after which entries are deleted automatically. Redact customer personal data in logs masks emails, addresses, phone numbers, and similar fields before they are stored. It is on by default. Record what AI assistants change keeps the before and after values of everything an assistant changes, encrypted, so you can review and undo it. It is on by default. Keep change history for (days) sets how long changes are kept, from 1 to 365. The default is 30 days. Save these with the Save Changes button at the bottom of the tab. See Activity for what gets recorded. Claude connector. Shown while the connector is on. Keep Claude connector sessions for sets how long a session on the remote connector URL can remain idle: 1 hour, 8 hours, or 24 hours. The default is 24 hours. Every message starts the wait again, so this is the longest break a session can take, not its maximum total lifetime. This setting applies to clients using the connector URL; the Claude Desktop MCPB bridge uses a separate adapter session. After a longer break, Claude starts a new session by itself, but a chat that was already open may not show the store’s tools again. Start a new chat to get them back. A shorter window ends idle sessions sooner. A session only works for the API key or connector URL that started it, and the stored session holds no key, so a longer window does not leave a usable credential in your database. Save it with Save Changes . Site readiness. Site readiness checks what your store can do and reports it for each AI service separately, so a store that is fine for ChatGPT and blocked for Claude reads as exactly that. The tab shows the last report, with when it ran. Select Verify site readiness to run it for the first time, or Check again for a fresh one. The report opens with the overall result and groups the checks beneath it: Your site holds the prerequisites every service shares: the MCP Adapter , the MCP for WooCommerce server (registered with the tools it should have, and answering at its address), the MCP for WooCommerce connector switch, Encryption for connector URLs , This plugin’s REST endpoints , and Reachable from the internet . One group per service holds the checks only that service can fail: Claude (its endpoint, streaming replies, the connector URL, and an OAuth conflict with another plugin), ChatGPT (its schema endpoint and import URL), Cursor , VS Code / GitHub Copilot , and Other AI services (the MCP endpoint, and whether the app will trust your HTTPS certificate). Hosting and security looks for settings that block AI apps: PHP errors printed into responses, a stripped X-MCP-API-Key header or ?token= query string, cached REST replies, a CDN or firewall in front of the site, security plugins, and other MCP plugins. The Other MCP plugins row names the MCP Adapter separately, as required: the plugin’s server runs on it, and the adapter’s own default server is a separate address that does not list this plugin’s tools. Each row carries a Pass, Warning, Fail, or Not checked result, and anything that is not a pass explains itself in place. Each group is collapsed until you open it. One caveat matters when you read a passing report. Every check runs from your site to itself, so none of them can see a firewall, a staging password, or an AI bot rule sitting between an assistant’s servers and your store. A pass means nothing on your side is in the way. Only a real connection proves an assistant can reach you. Site readiness also runs as a test under Tools > Site Health . Opening that screen runs a fresh check, which also updates the report on the Advanced tab, and the MCP details are on the Site Health Info tab. WordPress’s weekly background Site Health check leaves this test out, so it only runs when someone opens the Site Health screen. Manage API Keys. The WooCommerce REST API keys an assistant uses, with each key’s description, masked key, permission, and user. A client sends its key in the X-MCP-API-Key header. The key’s own permission controls what the assistant can do: a read key can only run read operations like search, list, and get, while write or read/write keys can also create, update, and delete. The user attached to the key must also have the manage_woocommerce capability. Create the most limited key that still does the job. Revoking a key from this list immediately cuts off any assistant that was using it — this is also how you disconnect an assistant. Actions menu. Every key in the list has an Actions menu, opened from the button at the end of its row. It holds everything that key can do: Copy MCP connector URL (Claude, ChatGPT app) and Copy schema URL (Custom GPT) — the key’s connector URL, in the form the client expects. One key works with every assistant, so both are always offered: the same token authenticates both addresses, and only the endpoint they point at differs. Claude and the ChatGPT app both take the MCP connector URL; only a Custom GPT wants the schema URL. The URL is available whenever you come back, so losing it is not a reason to create anything new. Regenerate URL — issue a fresh URL for that key. The previous one stops working immediately, so anyone using it is disconnected until you give them the new one. Every other key, and anyone using it, is unaffected. The confirmation that follows includes copy buttons so you can hand the new URL straight to the assistant. Disconnect URL — switch off that key’s URL while the key itself keeps working for clients that send it as a header, such as the Claude Desktop app. Revoke key — delete the API key outright. This cannot be undone, and it removes the connector URL with it. A key that has no connector URL simply shows fewer entries: only Revoke key . The Connection tab creates the URL while the newly issued full credential is available. The key list cannot recover that credential later to create a missing URL. To give someone their own URL through this screen, create a new API key in the connection steps. Developer note: The remote connector for Claude and ChatGPT has to replay an API key to the site on every request, so that credential is stored in your database — one entry per key that has a connector URL. Each entry is encrypted at rest using a key derived from your site’s WordPress salts, which live in wp-config.php rather than the database, so a database backup alone does not expose a usable key. Treat each one as a live credential. To revoke a connector, either use Disconnect URL in that key’s Actions menu, which removes only that URL, or Revoke key in the same menu, which removes both. Deactivating the plugin clears every stored connector credential. Stores that connected before connector URLs became per-key have one older, shared URL that is not tied to a single API key. It keeps working exactly as before, and nothing needs to be changed or re-pasted. It is shown under the API keys list as Shared connector URL , where you can copy it or turn it off once everyone using it has their own URL. This section walks you from a fresh install to a working connection. Which steps you follow depends on two things: the assistant you are connecting, and where your store runs (a public website on the internet, or a local site on your own computer). Read the prerequisites first, then jump to the section that matches your setup: Connect the Claude Desktop app to a public site Connect the Claude Desktop app to a local site Connect Claude.ai in the browser to a public site Giving each person their own connection Connect the ChatGPT app to a public site Connect a Custom GPT to a public site Connect a Custom GPT to a local site Connect Cursor or VS Code Connect another AI service All of these start the same way. Go to WooCommerce > Settings > MCP > Connection , make sure the MCP Adapter status shows no error, pick your environment (on a local site) and assistant, and create an API key. The key is shown once and is the credential the assistant uses. Create the most limited key that does the job: a read key for reporting, a write or read/write key only when the assistant needs to make changes. Every assistant has a Prompt tab in the connect step. It holds a setup prompt with your store’s address, your new API key, and the setup steps for that app. Copy it into the app you are connecting. An app that can change its own configuration, such as Claude Code, can apply it for you; otherwise, the prompt gives you the manual steps to follow. For Claude, one prompt covers Claude Code, the Claude Desktop app, and Claude.ai in the browser, and the app you paste it into uses the method it supports. The prompt asks the app to check that it reached the right store before it reads any products. The prompt includes your API key, so treat it like the key itself. It is only available right after you create a key: on a later visit, create a new key to get a prompt. A few things need to be true before a connection will work. Most failed setups trace back to one of these. For a public website (your live store on the internet): The MCP Adapter is active, or the Connection tab shows no error about it. The site must be reachable over HTTPS with a valid, trusted SSL certificate. A self-signed or expired certificate will fail. Your host, firewall, or CDN must pass the connector’s POST requests and session headers. If the client opens an optional SSE stream for server messages, streaming responses must also be allowed. A stream can stay open for up to an hour before reconnecting; that is separate from the session’s 24-hour default idle lifetime. Your host, firewall, or CDN must also let the assistant’s own requests through to /wp-json/w7s-mcp/ , and to /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp if you have configurations from before 2.0.0. Cloudflare and several hosting panels now ship a one-click setting that blocks AI bots, and it blocks the assistant you connected on purpose along with the crawlers you wanted to keep out. See Requests blocked by Cloudflare or your host . Your assistant account or workspace must allow the connection method you choose. Plan availability, administrative permissions, and menu names can change; check the assistant’s current setup requirements. For a local website (running on your own computer, for example in a tool like Local, MAMP, or Docker): Connecting locally is more involved and is aimed at developers comfortable with a terminal, with editing configuration files, and with a tunneling tool such as ngrok. On a local site, the Connection tab starts with an environment picker. Choose Local website (on your computer) in Step 1 and the instructions adapt to the local setup, including the extra certificate settings. Claude Desktop can talk to a local site directly through a bridge, with one extra setting for the local SSL certificates. See Connect the Claude Desktop app to a local site below. Hosted remote connectors, including Claude.ai and hosted ChatGPT connections, cannot reach a private localhost address. Expose the site or bridge through a tunnel for those routes. A desktop or CLI MCP client running locally can use your local network instead. See the local Custom GPT steps below for the route the Connection tab offers. Developer note: The plugin’s manual Claude Desktop instructions use Node.js 22 or newer and recommend its full npx path. A Node version or PATH problem is one possible startup failure; check the client’s error rather than assuming it is the cause whenever tools are missing. See the manual setup steps below. It helps to know what the pieces are before you wire them together. The MCP endpoint is the address an assistant connects to. MCP for WooCommerce serves it at /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/mcp . This is the value a bridge needs as its WP_API_URL . Pass the full endpoint, not just your site root. Passing only the root returns a 404 rest_no_route error. Configurations made before 2.0.0 use /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp , which keeps working. The API key authenticates each request. It is a WooCommerce REST API key in the form consumer_key:consumer_secret , sent in the X-MCP-API-Key header. The key’s permission scope is enforced on every call, so a read key cannot write no matter how a request is phrased. The user attached to the key also needs the manage_woocommerce capability. From there, clients connect in one of three shapes: A local bridge. Claude Desktop runs a small helper on your machine that speaks to your store and presents the tools to the app. With the one-click bundle, the bridge ships inside the bundle; with the manual setup, it is the @automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote package. The bridge reads the key from its local configuration and sends it as a header. Creating a connector URL also stores an encrypted replayable copy on the site, even if you ultimately use the Desktop bridge; see Manage API Keys . A remote connector. Hosted clients connect to the Claude-compatible route using Streamable HTTP, with JSON replies to POST requests and an optional SSE stream for server messages. The generated connector URL carries a revocable token instead of the raw API key. Each URL belongs to one API key, whose credential is stored on the site encrypted at rest so the proxy can authenticate its internal requests. A read-only key stays read-only through the connector. A direct MCP or OpenAPI client. Tools such as Cursor, VS Code, Cline, n8n, or your own integration talk to the MCP endpoint directly with the X-MCP-API-Key header, or import the OpenAPI 3.1 schema. See Connect another AI service . This is the most common setup, and in most cases it is one click. On a public site, the Claude connect step opens on One click (for Claude.ai in the browser); use the MCPB bundle tab for the Desktop download, or Manual , then Desktop app in the Manual connection dropdown, for a configuration file. One-click setup (recommended): In WooCommerce > Settings > MCP > Connection , choose Claude and create an API key. On the MCPB bundle tab, select Download Claude Desktop bundle (.mcpb) . The bundle is built with this store’s endpoint and your new key already filled in. Double-click the downloaded .mcpb file. Claude Desktop opens and registers the store automatically — there is no configuration file to edit. This needs Claude Desktop 0.13.37 or newer, and Node.js 18 or newer on the same computer. Back on the Connection tab, wait for the connect step to show Connected . The bundle contains your API key, so treat the file like a credential. If the file is ever shared, revoke that key in the Manage API Keys list on the Advanced tab and download a fresh bundle with a new key. Manual setup: If you prefer to configure Claude Desktop by hand, or the bundle tab is not shown on your server, select Manual , then Desktop app . The manual setup runs a bridge on your computer using the @automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote package. Select Copy Claude Desktop Config . This builds a ready-to-paste block with your endpoint and key already filled in. Open the Claude Desktop configuration file, claude_desktop_config.json , and merge the block into its mcpServers section. See Find the Claude Desktop configuration file below if you are not sure where it is. The block looks similar to this: {
  "mcpServers": {
    "woocommerce-mcp": {
      "command": "/path/to/node22/bin/npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@automattic/mcp-wordpress-remote"],
      "env": {
        "WP_API_URL": "https://yourstore.com/wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/mcp",
        "CUSTOM_HEADERS": "{\"X-MCP-API-Key\": \"ck_yourkey:cs_yoursecret\"}"
      }
    }
  }
} Replace /path/to/node22/bin/npx with the real path on your computer. These instructions use Node.js 22 or newer, matching the plugin’s manual setup guidance. Claude Desktop may have a different PATH from your terminal, so use the full path. If you use nvm, run nvm use 22 , then which npx , and paste what it prints — for example /Users/you/.nvm/versions/node/v22.22.0/bin/npx . The upstream package currently declares Node.js 18 as its minimum; check its package requirements when troubleshooting a different installed version. Save the file, then fully quit and reopen Claude Desktop. A restart is required for it to pick up the change. In Claude Desktop, go to Settings > Developer > woocommerce-mcp and check that the status shows Running . The connect step on the Connection tab shows Connected once the first request arrives. Fully quit and reopen the app after changing its configuration. A configuration made before 2.0.0, with WP_API_URL ending in /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp , keeps working. You do not need to change it. The manual setup above asks you to edit claude_desktop_config.json . The easiest way to open it is from inside Claude Desktop, which also creates the file the first time if it does not exist yet. Open Claude Desktop. Go to Settings, then the Developer section. Select Edit Config . This opens claude_desktop_config.json in your default text editor. If the file is new, it may be empty or contain only {} . Add the mcpServers block inside the top-level braces. If mcpServers already exists with other servers in it, add woocommerce-mcp alongside them rather than replacing the whole section. If you would rather open the file directly, it lives here: macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json . The Library folder is hidden in Finder. Use Go, then Go to Folder (Shift+Cmd+G), and paste the path. Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json . Paste that into the File Explorer address bar or the Run dialog (Win+R). A missing comma or bracket will silently disable every server in the file, so check the JSON is valid if nothing loads. A tool pack is a group of related abilities, such as everything to do with orders or everything to do with products. If someone has changed one of those fields since, Undo stops and shows the value it would restore beside the current one, and only Overwrite replaces it, after asking again. Undoing a new item moves it to the trash, and undoing a move to the trash restores the item. An undo is a change in its own right: it is listed with “Undo of change #N”, the original change is marked Undone , and an undo can itself be undone. Undo runs with your permissions at the time: you need to be able to edit that item yourself, as well as manage WooCommerce. While it restores values, the store sends no emails, takes no payments, moves no stock, and schedules nothing. If an undo fails, it changes nothing and can be tried again. Rarely, another plugin saves its own work part-way through an undo, so part of it is kept even though the undo failed. Undo then says the item may be partly restored, and that change shows as unavailable to undo: check the item and correct it by hand. The item no longer exists to restore; only a move to the trash can be undone. Refunds, order status changes and payment details. Changes that could not be stored whole : a record cut short because it was very large, or saved without encryption because your server lacks it. Changes from a call that was not fully recorded , unless putting that one item back is safe on its own. The badge rows themselves , and changes already undone. Tested adapter versions are 0.3 (bundled with WooCommerce up to 11.2), 0.6.1 (bundled with Elementor), and 0.7. Authentication is a WooCommerce REST API key in X-MCP-API-Key only; the key’s scope is enforced on the parsed JSON-RPC message, batches included, and the key’s user needs manage_woocommerce . Application Passwords and cookie sessions are not accepted. Plain HTTP is refused unless w7s_mcp_allow_insecure_transport allows it. /wp-json/woocommerce/mcp is kept for configurations made before 2.0.0. A request carrying X-MCP-API-Key is handed to the plugin’s server; any other request goes to WooCommerce’s own handler (HTTP 410 from WooCommerce 11.3). The route is added when WooCommerce does not register it. Requests are counted per API key ID for WooCommerce > Status , kept for 30 days. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-legacy-endpoint.php . /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/claude/mcp is the Streamable HTTP connector proxy; /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/claude/sse is an alias for existing URLs. It accepts a connector token ( ?token= ), X-MCP-API-Key , or the legacy ?api_key= parameter, and forwards requests to the plugin’s MCP server. The ChatGPT schema at /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/chatgpt/openapi.json accepts the same credential forms for import. Custom GPT tool calls use /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/chatgpt/tools/<tool> with the configured API key header. /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/connection/health runs site readiness. It needs the manage_options capability, like the API key routes. /wp-json/w7s-mcp/v1/site-health runs the same checks for the Tools > Site Health test, and needs view_site_health_checks . The test sets skip_cron , so WordPress’s weekly Site Health cron, which runs tests in-process without a REST route, leaves it out. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-site-health.php . The plugin’s abilities register only on its MCP routes, its two readiness routes, and inside Store Control. They default to meta.mcp.public = false and show_in_rest = false , keeping them off the MCP Adapter’s default server and the Abilities REST API. Without an adapter, the direct MCP routes answer HTTP 503 with a JSON-RPC error (code -32000 ) asking for the MCP Adapter; the Claude and ChatGPT proxies also report the missing adapter. Store Control can still run tools inside the site without an adapter. w7s_mcp_include_ability (filter) decides whether an ability is on the plugin’s server. It receives bool $include and string $ability_id , and runs after Tool Packs. It replaces WooCommerce’s woocommerce_mcp_include_ability , which WooCommerce 11.3 drops. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-tool-list.php . w7s_mcp_server_tools (filter) receives the final list of ability IDs the server is created with, after Tool Packs and w7s_mcp_include_ability . Every ID is revalidated afterwards: unregistered, REST-derived, and duplicate entries are dropped, and the nine core tools always keep their names. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-tool-list.php . w7s_mcp_allow_insecure_transport (filter) decides whether an MCP request may arrive over plain HTTP. It receives bool $allow and the WP_REST_Request . Its default is the value of WooCommerce’s woocommerce_mcp_allow_insecure_transport filter, so existing local setups keep working. Use it on local development sites only. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-authorizer.php . w7s_mcp_legacy_endpoint_enabled (filter) decides whether the plugin serves the woocommerce/mcp compatibility address. Default true . When false , the route is left exactly as WooCommerce registers it, and clients configured with the old address stop reaching the plugin’s server. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-legacy-endpoint.php . woocommerce_mcp_include_ability is deprecated. MCP for WooCommerce still applies it to its own server for one release, through apply_filters_deprecated() with a notice pointing at w7s_mcp_include_ability . Move your callbacks to w7s_mcp_include_ability . The current connector speaks the session-based MCP revisions 2025-11-25 , 2025-06-18 , 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05 . It echoes a supported proposal and otherwise offers 2025-11-25 . The protocol the proxy negotiates with its upstream adapter is stored separately from the client-facing version. Initialize: opens a new connector and upstream session. The HTTP 200 JSON-RPC result contains only protocolVersion , capabilities and serverInfo ; it does not embed tools or toolsNextCursor or fetch the catalogue eagerly. The response supplies MCP-Session-Id . Initialized notification: a POST without an ID is accepted with HTTP 202 and no JSON-RPC response body. It is not forwarded as an upstream request. Discovery and execution: the client requests tools/list and tools/call separately. Tool schemas and annotations are normalized on tools/list. Optional GET stream: a client can listen for server messages using Mcp-Session-Id , or the legacy session_id query parameter. The stream closes after at most 3,600 seconds; closing it does not delete the session. An ordinary browser GET without a session receives HTTP 400 with an explanation. Session termination: DELETE with a valid session header returns HTTP 204. An expired or unknown session returns HTTP 404 so the client can initialize again. Modern discovery probes: the connector does not implement the stateless 2026-07-28 protocol. A session-less modern request such as server/discover receives HTTP 400 with JSON-RPC -32600 , allowing a client that supports both eras to fall back to initialize. This is not an advertisement of modern protocol support. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-claude-sse.php and includes/class-w7s-mcp-protocol-version.php . w7s_mcp_session_ttl (filter) sets how long a Claude connector session survives without a message, in seconds. It receives the window chosen on the Advanced tab, 86400 (24 hours) by default. The result is kept between 300 seconds and 30 days. Every message starts the wait again. A session past the MCP Adapter’s own 24-hour inactivity timeout keeps working, because the plugin starts a new adapter session when the adapter rejects the old one. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-claude-sse.php . A Claude connector session is stored as a transient named w7s_mcp_sse_<session id> . New records hold a keyed hash of the API key, the upstream adapter session, a tool-list revision, and timestamps; they do not retain the credential or queued tool responses. A session opened through a connector URL also records a hash of its token. A later request may authenticate with only the session ID while that connector URL remains valid; replacing or removing the URL ends that access. Header-authenticated sessions require the key on every request. Another key receives HTTP 404, as for an expired session. When a legacy record still contains its credential, the loader tries to associate it with a live connector URL before dropping the credential. Session-only access continues if that association succeeds; otherwise the client must supply its credential or start a new session. w7s_mcp_chatgpt_max_operations (filter) controls how many operations the Custom GPT schema includes; the default is 30. Values below 1 disable server-side trimming for inspection or another compatible OpenAPI client, but do not change the importing client’s limits or the Tool Packs UI’s Custom GPT selection limit. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-chatgpt-openapi.php . w7s_mcp_connector_enabled (filter) is the master switch returned by W7S_MCP::is_connector_enabled() . When it resolves to false , assistant access to MCP and ChatGPT tools is disabled and the assistant-facing tabs are hidden. Administrative settings and readiness remain available. It defaults to the stored connector option. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp.php . w7s_mcp_register_tool_packs (action) fires when tool packs are collected. It passes a $register callable, so another plugin can add a pack that admins then switch on or off in Tool Packs: add_action( 'w7s_mcp_register_tool_packs', function ( $register ) {
    $register(
        'my_plugin_slug',
        __( 'My Plugin', 'my-plugin' ),
        __( 'Description.', 'my-plugin' ),
        'my_plugin/ability_prefix'
    );
} ); Abilities whose ID starts with that prefix are included on the plugin’s MCP server only while the pack is enabled. They need no mcp meta of their own. The callable also accepts optional per-ability descriptors (for per-ability toggles), a plugin label, and a category label. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-tool-packs.php . Individual abilities are registered with the WordPress Abilities API, not with a plugin-specific hook. Register them with wp_register_ability , then either register a pack for their prefix, which gives store owners a switch, or let the store owner add them from the Add tools tab. To include an ability without a pack, use w7s_mcp_include_ability . Read-only key enforcement relies on two classifiers, both filterable, in includes/class-w7s-mcp-ability-helper.php : w7s_mcp_is_write_operation decides whether a given ability or tool name counts as a write. The plugin classifies by name (write verbs such as create , update , delete , batch ; read verbs such as get , list , search ). Anything unrecognized defaults to write, so an unknown tool cannot be run by a read-only key. Use this filter to correct the classification for a custom tool. w7s_mcp_is_destructive_ability overrides whether an ability is treated as destructive. The plugin first trusts an explicit destructive declaration from the Abilities API, then falls back to name heuristics. Scope is also checked where each of the plugin’s own abilities runs, in front of its permission callback, so it does not rest on request parsing alone. w7s_mcp_readiness_services (filter) receives the list of services site readiness reports on, so another plugin can add its own assistant beside the built-in ones. Each entry implements W7S_MCP_Readiness_Service ( includes/readiness/interface-w7s-mcp-readiness-service.php ), which is three methods: get_id() returns a stable slug used as the key in the REST response and as the prefix for the service’s check ids, get_label() its merchant-facing name, and run( $context ) returns its check results. The runner establishes the shared prerequisites once and passes them in as $context , so a service never re-probes what the runner has already settled. Anything a service cannot test because a prerequisite failed should come back as a skipped check rather than a passing one. Build results with the W7S_MCP_Readiness_Check factories ( ok() , warning() , fail() , skipped() ), each taking a stable untranslated id, a translated label, an explanation, and an optional untranslated support detail such as HTTP 401 . A service that throws is reported as failed rather than taking the readiness response down with it. Source: includes/readiness/class-w7s-mcp-readiness.php . Writes through the WordPress tools are restricted to allowlists, all filterable, in includes/class-w7s-mcp-wordpress-tools.php : w7s_mcp_writable_option_keys controls which options may be written. w7s_mcp_writable_post_fields controls which post fields may be written. w7s_mcp_allowed_protected_post_meta allows specific protected meta keys (defaults to _thumbnail_id ). w7s_mcp_max_upload_bytes caps the maximum upload size in bytes. The action log records MCP tool calls, along with the response each one returned, and masks PII before storage. w7s_mcp_log_pii_arg_keys (filter) adjusts which keys are redacted, so you can add custom checkout meta or remove a default. The same key list governs the response: MCP returns its payload as a JSON string inside a text part, so the log decodes that string before redacting, and a customer field buried in a tool’s output is masked the same way as one in its arguments. Source: includes/class-w7s-mcp-action-log.php . The log is viewable under Activity → Tool calls. Logging is on by default and retention defaults to 7 days, clamped to between 1 and 365; both are configurable on the Advanced tab, and a daily cron ( w7s_mcp_clean_old_logs ) applies the retention. Three filters shape what the in-admin chat sends to the AI provider, all in includes/client/class-w7s-mcp-chat-client.php : w7s_mcp_chat_tool_result_char_budget sets the character budget for a single tool result before it is cut at item boundaries (default 12,000, floored at 500). Larger results carry a truncated note stating the real total. w7s_mcp_chat_scrub_tool_args filters the arguments the model supplied before a tool runs. It receives the scrubbed arguments, the tool name, and the original arguments. w7s_mcp_chat_tool_description filters the description a tool is advertised with, so you can steer how the model chooses between them. Use Activity → Tool calls for executed tools and WooCommerce > Status > Logs , source w7s-mcp-claude , for the connector handshake. The latter records request methods, negotiated versions, session-header presence, tool counts and outcomes without logging the token or API key. Several Anthropic client identities may initialize separately. WordPress can also invoke a permission callback repeatedly while building the Allow header, so repeated authentication lines are not separate connections. Errors registering the plugin’s MCP server appear as MCP server last error in WooCommerce > Status . An SDK test that passes from your machine does not establish that a hosted assistant’s runtime connected; verify an actual tool result in that assistant. For a source checkout with dependencies installed, the read-only diagnostic at tests/integration/claude-connector-check.mjs checks the real HTTP initialize response, SDK connection, tool list and a coupon-list call. Set W7S_CLAUDE_CONNECTOR_URL in the gitignored tests/.env.integration file, then run: node tests/integration/claude-connector-check.mjs It prints response metadata and validation failures without the token or coupon data. The coupon-list tool must be enabled. This developer script lives in the source repository and is not included in the installed plugin ZIP. Protocol (MCP) client to your store’s WooCommerce AI server. Use the endpoint generated for your store, then authorize the client and confirm a read-only request before allowing store changes. Note : This is a Developer level doc. If you are unfamiliar working with code and resolving potential conflicts, we recommend you work with a Woo Agency Partner for larger projects, or find a WooCommerce developer on Codeable for smaller customizations. We are unable to provide support for customizations under our Support Policy . WooCommerce and WooCommerce AI are active. Your store and user account are connected to WordPress.com. Your account can manage WooCommerce. The MCP client supports remote HTTP servers and the authentication flow used by the endpoint. In WordPress admin, go to WooCommerce > Settings > WooCommerce AI > Advanced > MCP server . Enable Progressive MCP server if it is off. Open Setup , choose your client, and copy the generated server URL or configuration. The WordPress.com URL includes your store identifier. Its structure is: https://public-api.wordpress.com/wpcom/v2/sites/{site}/woocommerce-ai-mcp/v1 Copy the complete URL from your store’s Setup screen, including its store identifier. Follow Claude Code’s MCP instructions for your installed client version. Add the copied endpoint with: claude mcp add --transport http woocommerce-ai "YOUR_COPIED_SERVER_URL" In Claude Code, open /mcp and complete the authentication flow when prompted. The WordPress.com connection uses OAuth on first use; this path does not require copying a WooCommerce consumer secret into the client configuration. Confirm that the client lists the server as connected and discovers its tools. Start with a read-only store query and compare the returned result with WordPress admin. If authentication or discovery fails, check the copied endpoint, site and user connection, and the client’s error before retrying. Return to the MCP server settings to enable or disable the tools exposed to external clients. Changes save as you change the controls. A disabled tool is removed from discovery and rejected if a client tries to use it. These controls are distinct from chat ability settings . Combined exposure groups read tools behind the load-provider and execute-tool helpers. In this mode, the settings table shows those two helpers with fixed, disabled toggles. Individual exposure lists tools directly and provides per-tool controls. After changing the exposure mode, refresh the client’s tool list to see the available tools. Developers can connect directly to the store endpoint using a WooCommerce REST API key. Use the endpoint: https://your-store.example/wp-json/woocommerce-ai/mcp The direct transport accepts the X-MCP-API-Key header in consumer_key:consumer_secret format. Use a dedicated key with the least required permission and keep its secret in the client’s supported secure configuration. Read keys permit read operations; write or read/write keys permit the corresponding writes. Keep the key out of screenshots and shared files. Follow your client’s official instructions for adding the API-key header.
